correctness.rationale: Unnormalized Fourier intensity is the discrete Fourier transform of integer periodic autocorrelation; the orbit enumeration searches every translated/reflected/global-sign version and covers all signals by anchoring a nonzero entry. Exact full census at orders 5,7,11 produces spectra 6,26,135 and orbit classes 6,26,140, with exactly five two-orbit fibers at 11. An independent all-5280-signals order-11 census confirms completeness. Infinite-prime ambiguity follows from an exact polynomial reciprocal-factor identity and a combinatorial orbit obstruction valid for every prime at least 11.

originality.rationale: The closest published finite-alphabet theorem assumes generic nonzero letters and explicitly does not furnish complete recovery classifications. The fixed letters +1,-1 are non-generic; their first ambiguous prime order and all first fibers are not implied by this theorem. Signed difference sets require constant nonzero autocorrelation, unlike the exhibited profiles. Classical unsigned four-set homometry does not contain prime 11, whereas signed signals do. Published sparse Fourier-zero papers treat vanishing Fourier coefficients, not equality of the entire power spectrum; frequency-deletion measurements are also different.
residual_risks: An older catalog of signed periodic homometric sequences may already tabulate the entire order-11 census in different terminology.
The universal zero-flip polynomial construction may be classical; the claimed new contribution is the sharp first prime and complete five exceptional fiber classification in the fixed alphabet.
Publication databases and search cannot rule out all equivalent or stronger statements.

value.rationale: The non-generic sign alphabet is motivated by finite-alphabet crystallographic phase retrieval. The least prime order allowing a nontrivial signed four-atom ambiguity is an exact natural sampling threshold, and all five ambiguous power spectra and fiber sizes at that first order are classified. This is not merely a factorization example: the result combines a complete first-threshold census with a uniform algebraic witness for all larger primes, providing a precise boundary for unique signed sparse recovery.
